From: Jake Dalton <jdalton@buckeyeaz.gov> 
Sent: Wednesday, February 11, 2026 12:19 PM
To: Steve Skye <steve@christysigns.com>
Subject: BLDC-26-0049 - Structural design and calculations required

 

Hi Steve,

I wanted to follow up regarding the sign submittal on BLDC-26-0049. I received clarification from my supervisors after our conversation on the “per ASA requirements” note. While we understand that reference may have been used on prior projects, we are not able to approve the sign based on that note alone. 

The current plans do not include enough structural information to verify compliance (e.g., sign structure member sizing/materials, anchorage/base-plate details, foundation/footing design, and applicable design criteria). To proceed, please submit structural plans and supporting calculations for the sign structure and foundation/anchorage. Documents must be prepared by a design professional, as applicable, and should clearly indicate the design criteria used (wind, exposure, etc.) along with all connection and footing details.

 

 

 <https://www.buckeyeaz.gov/> 

Jacob Dalton
Building Plans Examiner I

subject: The Mix on Roosevelt – Engineering Clarification (02/11/26)
body:
Hi Jake,



Thank you again for taking the time to speak with me regarding the proposed monument sign at The Mix on Roosevelt.


I wanted to follow up to clarify one item from our plans. The engineering details referenced on the drawings are based on specifications provided through the Arizona Sign Association (ASA). As a member of ASA, Christy Signs utilizes their standard engineering criteria for our structural submittals.


Our plans currently cite this simply as “ASA,” and I understand that may not have been immediately clear. The engineering provided does meet ASA standards, and we will make this reference more explicit on future submittals for clarity.


Thank you again for your time and assistance.


Warm regards,

 

Steve Skye

subject: Burros & Fries – CSP / Sign Code Conflict Update (02/11/26)
body:
Hi Rocky,



I wanted to discuss with you the recent correspondence with Dana Stevens, Planning Specialist for the Town of Gilbert regarding the Burros & Fries sign permit application.



Planning has clarified their position that the Comprehensive Sign Plan (CSP) does not authorize signage beyond what the Gilbert sign code allows. In short, they are requiring the wall signs to meet base code limits, even though the CSP exhibits depict larger approved sign areas.  

 

This creates a procedural conflict between:

*	The stamped CSP exhibits (approved December 17, 2025), and
*	Planning’s current interpretation that the CSP does not override code allowances.


At this point, we have two possible paths:

1.	Obtain formal clarification from Planning confirming whether the CSP was intended to modify sign allowances, or
2.	Revise the CPS removing the generic language concerning adhering to the Gilbert sign code.


I have placed calls to the Town of Gilbert Planning Department to obtain additional clarity on how CSP approvals are intended to function relative to the sign ordinance. I am waiting for a return call so we can determine the correct course before making design adjustments.


I’ll update you as soon as I receive further guidance.


Regards,

Hi Dana,



I wanted to follow up after reviewing the Notice of Decision and its attachments more closely. I appreciate you flagging that language.


After review, we do see that the Sign Plan Text includes general language stating that signage must conform to the sign code. At the same time, the Notice of Decision states that construction of the signs shall conform to the exhibits submitted for the request, which were stamped administratively approved on December 17, 2025. subject: First Watch – Queen Creek | Sign Permit Corrections & Required Revisions (02/04/26)
body:
Hi Scott,



We’ve received the correction comments from the Town of Queen Creek for the First Watch – Harvest Station sign permit.


The Planning review is complete, and the project is currently on hold pending revisions. I’ve attached the following for reference:

*	Town of Queen Creek Corrections Report
*	Harvest Station Comprehensive Sign Plan (CSP)
*	Current First Watch sign drawings and elevations


In summary, the Town is requiring revisions in two key areas:

1.	Wall Sign / Raceway Design
	The proposed wall signs do not currently meet the CSP requirement for architecturally integrated raceways. The CSP requires individual channel letters integrated into a designed signage wireway or sign band that is complementary to the building architecture, rather than a standard exposed raceway. The sign details and elevations will need to be revised accordingly.
2.	Sign Area Calculations
	The submittal must clearly document building frontage dimensions and provide sign area calculations per the CSP (1.5 SF per linear foot, max 250 SF per building). These calculations need to be shown directly on the plans.


Once the sign design and calculations are updated, we can prepare a full resubmittal package and response letter addressing each comment.  Let me know if able to be of any additional assistance.

Great question.



For Avondale, once the sign permit is issued, it remains valid as long as the project stays active. Specifically:



*	The permit will expire if no inspections are requested and approved within 180 days of issuance, or
*	If work becomes inactive for 180 consecutive days after issuance.


As long as we schedule inspections within that window, the permit stays active, even if production hasn’t started immediately.

subject: Inspector Request – Photo Documentation for Legacy U-Haul Permit (Mesa) (01/27/26)
body:
Team,



I wanted to document a conversation I had this morning with Gilbert Chavez, Temp Building Inspector II with the City of Mesa, regarding a legacy permit:



Record: PMT19-11810
Project: U-Haul
Address: 457 S Higley Rd, Mesa, AZ 85206


Gilbert advised that, as part of closing out inspections on this older permit, the city is requesting photo documentation showing:



*	The electrical disconnect switch serving the sign
*	The primary conductors properly secured and supported
	
	

From a code standpoint, these requests align with the adopted 2023 NEC, including:



*	NEC 600.6 – Disconnecting means required for electric signs
*	NEC 300.11 – Securing and supporting of raceways and conductors
*	NEC 110.12 – Mechanical execution of work (general workmanship)


Gilbert indicated that providing clear photo documentation of these items will allow the city to verify compliance without additional site visits, which is increasingly how Mesa (and other jurisdictions) are handling follow-up on legacy permits.


As a broader takeaway, this is another example of why photo surveys are becoming standard practice. Having organized, labeled photo documentation readily available goes a long way in:



*	facilitating required inspections,
*	reducing back-and-forth with inspectors,
*	and building long-term goodwill with jurisdictions and inspection staff.


Moving forward, continuing to treat photo surveys as a standard part of our process—especially for electrical and serviceability items—will help streamline closeouts like this.


I’ll coordinate the requested photos for this permit and keep everyone posted if anything further is needed.


Thanks,



Steve Skye

subject: On-Site Findings – Budweiser Building Sign Access (01/26/26)
body:
Hi Dan,



Our crews were on site at the facility to troubleshoot the illuminated Budweiser building sign.


Upon investigation, we determined that the sign is not serviceable due to blocked access. Interior access to the sign cavity is obstructed by permanent structural steel members, roof framing, and building components. As documented in the attached interior photos and summarized in the attached photo survey report, these obstructions prevent safe or practical entry to the sign electrical components. There is no existing service opening or removable access panel that would allow maintenance from within the building.


As a result, troubleshooting, repair, or future servicing of this sign cannot be performed without modifications to the existing structure or the creation of a dedicated access point designed specifically for sign maintenance.


Please review the attached Photo Survey Report and advise how you would like to proceed. We can provide recommendations and options for creating compliant service access if needed.


Best regards,

 

Steve Skye

Fax: 602-271-0433

body:
Hi Sarah,



I hope you’re doing well.


Attached are the proposed wall sign options for the new BMS Moving & Storage location for your review. We’ve included two design variations, one of which incorporates an outline to demonstrate how the sign reads more clearly against the building façade.

subject: The Mix on Roosevelt – Permit Status Clarification Needed (01/22/26)
body:
Hi Rocky,



I wanted to update you after having an extended conversation with the City of Buckeye Planning Department regarding The Mix on Roosevelt project.


The Planning staff conducted a detailed search of their records and were unable to locate any sign permit application for this project. The technicians I spoke with are familiar with the site, but they do not see any record of submitted plans for pylon signs that correspond with those shown on the attached artwork.


Based on their review, it appears there is no sign application on file for this. This raises the possibility that the application may never have been formally submitted, or that it was submitted under a different project name or address that we are not currently aware of.


Please advise how you would like to proceed. Once we confirm the intended path forward, I can coordinate next steps with the city to get this moving correctly.

subject: Living Waters Church – Electrical Permit & Power Coordination (01/21/26)
body:
Hi Mike,



It was good speaking with you earlier. I wanted to follow up with the details on the Living Waters Church pole sign project and outline what is needed to move it forward.


The sign permit is otherwise complete and in its final stage of approval. The only remaining requirement for the Town to release the sign permit is issuance of the electrical permit for primary power to the base of the pole sign.


Scope Needed

*	Obtain the electrical permit for power to the base of the pole sign
*	Secure and provide primary power at the base of the sign in accordance with what you propose and submit to the Town
*	Coordinate directly with the Town of Chino Valley Building Division as needed


Please note: Your electrical work and permitting will be contracted directly with Living Waters Church.


Electrical Load Information (Already Defined)

The electrical load for the sign has already been established for permitting purposes as follows:

*	Maximum power consumption: 1,705.6 watts
*	At 120 volts: approximately 14.5 amps
*	At 208 volts: approximately 8.5 amps
*	Top cabinet power: 60-watt power supply
*	At 120 volts, the load remains well within the 80% capacity threshold, allowing the use of a 120-volt photocell to control the top cabinet illumination


Town of Chino Valley – Building Division
Heather Narvesen, Senior Permit Technician
📞 928-636-3480
✉️ hnarvesen@chinoaz.net

I’ve attached the proposed sign drawings for your reference. These plans have already been reviewed and will be approved immediately once the electrical permit is issued.


If you need any additional information (site details, load clarification, or coordination assistance with the Town), feel free to reach out and I’ll get it to you right away.


Thanks again for your help on this.

subject: State Farm – Brayden Hough | Gilbert Corrections Summary (SIGN-2025-00341) (01/20/26)
body:
Hi Cassidy,



The Town of Gilbert has returned Permit #SIGN-2025-00341 for corrections. Attached is the reviewer markup for reference.  Main items to address on the resubmittal:



*	Sign area: Reviewer indicates the proposed 15 sq. ft. exceeds what is allowed under the Higley Pecos Retail CSP and Town code—we’ll need to confirm the allowable sign area for this tenant space and revise the sign size accordingly.
*	Raceway not allowed: The reviewer notes raceways are prohibited for this center/CSP, so the sign will need to be revised to no raceway (typically flush-mount / concealed wiring).
*	Provide mounting/profile detail: The reviewer requests a side mounting profile / installation detail (projection, attachment method, and how wiring will be concealed) for review.
*	No exposed equipment: Notes indicate no exposed tubing, conduit, or raceways—conductors/transformers/equipment must be concealed.
*	Confirm CSP-compliant letter construction: Drawings should clearly call out individual pan channel letters per CSP requirements (materials/returns/illumination) and remove any conflicting notes.


Let me know if you want us to help confirm the allowable sign area for this suite and coordinate the revised drawing set for resubmittal.

subject: RE: Crumbl–Peoria - Allowed Sign Area Confirmation (01/16/26)
body:
Hi Sarah,



Thanks for the question — this is a good one.


I reviewed both the City of Phoenix Sign Ordinance and the Metro Towne Center Comprehensive Sign Plan (CSP) to confirm the allowable sign area for this location.


Although the tenant frontage is approximately 25 feet, the City of Phoenix code provides a minimum wall sign allowance of 50 square feet for commercial tenants. This comes directly from Phoenix Sign Ordinance Table D-1, which states:



“Wall Signs – Commercial: 1 square foot of sign area per 1 linear foot of building frontage (minimum 50 square feet).”


Because the ordinance establishes a 50 sq ft minimum, the normal frontage-based calculation (25 LF = 25 sq ft) does not apply here.


The Metro Towne Center CSP does not reduce this allowance — it regulates sign type and design standards, not overall area. The CSP permits aluminum pan channel letters for shop tenants and defers to the city ordinance for allowable square footage.  Based on both the Phoenix Sign Ordinance and the CSP:



• The maximum allowable area for the Crumbl primary wall sign is 50 square feet
• This allowance applies even with a 25’ tenant frontage
• Flush-mounted channel letters up to 50 sq ft total are permitted


You can therefore size the letters and logo however needed, provided the overall sign copy fits within a 50 sq ft envelope.


Please let us know if able to be of any additional assistance.

Subject: RE: Crumbl – Metro Towne Center CSP Review & Design Direction (01/13/26) 

 

Sarah,


Yes — your understanding is correct.


Under the Metro Towne Center CSP, the key requirement is that the sign copy be aluminum pan channel letters and not a cabinet-style sign box. 

The CSP does not prohibit raceways or backer panels — it regulates the sign type, not whether the letters are mounted directly to the wall, to a mesh raceway, or to a solid raceway.


Tropical Smoothie is a good example of this. Their sign uses individual channel letters mounted to a solid raceway, which is allowed under the CSP, just as the mesh-style raceways used by Supercuts, Pizza Patrón, and Dickey’s are allowed. Crumbl can follow either approach.


So, for Crumbl:

*	The letters must be individual aluminum pan channel letters
*	They may be mounted to a painted mesh or solid raceway
*	The raceway should be painted to match the wall or approved background color
*	A beige background will be acceptable, subject to City approval, just as it is for Tropical Smoothie


As long as the drawings clearly show channel letters on a painted raceway (not a cabinet), the design will be CSP-compliant and should satisfy the City’s correction without requiring a Minor Amendment.

Hi Sarah,

We received the Metro Towne Center Comprehensive Sign Plan (CSP) from the City of Phoenix today and completed our review in response to the EPR correction on the Crumbl – Peoria project.


Based on the CSP, we found the following with respect to the City’s comments:


The CSP prohibits cabinet-style sign boxes, but it allows tenant signage to be constructed as individually mounted aluminum pan channel letters. The CSP regulates the sign copy type, not the mounting method, and it does not prohibit raceways.


We have attached a CSP Compliance Exhibit documenting multiple existing tenants at Metro Towne Center — including Supercuts, Pizza Patrón, Dickey’s Barbecue Pit, Cold Stone, and MetroPCS — all of which use individual LED channel letters mounted to mesh or box raceways. These were approved under the same CSP and establish the accepted construction standard for this center. Accordingly, the Crumbl sign will be CSP-compliant when constructed as:

• Individually illuminated aluminum pan channel letters
• Mounted to a painted mesh or box raceway consistent with existing tenants
• No cabinet or translucent sign box
• Installed within the approved building sign band


This configuration satisfies both the CSP and the City’s correction and does not require a Minor Amendment.

subject: FW: Uni K Wax – Scottsdale Plan Review Corrections (Cycle 2)
body:
Hi Sarah,



Forwarding the City of Scottsdale plan review response for Uni K Wax. The review came back as Corrections on Cycle 2.


The main items noted by the reviewer are as follows:



*	Sign area compliance:
	The total sign area needs to remain within the allowable square footage based on storefront width. The reviewer noted that the directory/front-lit sign elevation exceeds the remaining allowed area, so the sign sizes will need to be reduced to keep the total at or below the 20 SF maximum.
*	Storefront width / percentage clarification:
	Overall sign length must not exceed 75% of the storefront width, and the calculations need to clearly demonstrate compliance.
*	Elevation clarification:
	There is a note questioning the elevation labeling (east vs. north). The elevations should be clearly identified and consistent across the drawings.


I’ve attached the correction report and marked-up plans for reference.



Let me know if you want to walk through the comments together before revising.

Hi Sarah,

We received the Metro Towne Center Comprehensive Sign Plan (CSP) from the City of Phoenix today and completed our review in response to the EPR correction on the Crumbl – Peoria project.


Based on the CSP, we found the following with respect to the City’s comments:


The CSP prohibits cabinet-style sign boxes, but it allows tenant signage to be constructed as individually mounted aluminum pan channel letters. The CSP regulates the sign copy type, not the mounting method, and it does not prohibit raceways.


We have attached a CSP Compliance Exhibit documenting multiple existing tenants at Metro Towne Center — including Supercuts, Pizza Patrón, Dickey’s Barbecue Pit, Cold Stone, and MetroPCS — all of which use individual LED channel letters mounted to mesh or box raceways. • Individually illuminated aluminum pan channel letters
• Mounted to a painted mesh or box raceway consistent with existing tenants
• No cabinet or translucent sign box
• Installed within the approved building sign band


This configuration satisfies both the CSP and the City’s correction and does not require a Minor Amendment.


Once Silicone Signs updates the drawings to this configuration, we can proceed with resubmitting the package to EPR.

subject: FW: Applicant Resubmit - EPR Task Assignment for 251558-LPSG
body:
Hi Sarah,


We received EPR corrections from the City of Phoenix for Crumbl – Peoria (Job #27461), and I wanted to bring you up to speed.


The reviewer noted that this project is governed by the Metro Towne Center Comprehensive Sign Plan (CSP). Per their comments, cabinet signs are not permitted, and the CSP currently allows aluminum pan channel letters only. To proceed as-is, the sign would need to be revised to comply, or alternatively, a Minor Amendment could be pursued (which would require a narrative, additional review time, and a $270 fee).


That said, during our photo survey we did observe nearby tenant signs within the same center that appear to utilize mesh or open backers, which may indicate some flexibility under the CSP. Because of that, I’ve reached out to the City of Phoenix Sign Services Department (pdd.signservices@phoenix.gov <mailto:pdd.signservices@phoenix.gov> ) requesting clarification and asking how we can obtain a copy of the Metro Towne Center CSP for review.


Once we receive the CSP details or confirmation from the City, we’ll have a clearer path on whether a compliant mesh/backer option is feasible or if a formal amendment would be required.


I’ll keep you posted as soon as we hear back.


Best regards,



Steve Skye

subject: Subject: Outlook Tasks / To Do Missing After Microsoft Platform Upgrade
body:
Rocky,



We’re reporting an issue with Outlook Tasks / Microsoft To Do for the mailbox steve@christysigns.com that appears to have occurred following a Microsoft Outlook / Exchange platform upgrade, not due to user changes.


After troubleshooting across:

*	Outlook (Classic – Windows)
*	Outlook (New – Windows 11)
*	Microsoft To Do (web)
*	Edge and Chrome
*	Password, passkey, and one-time code authentication

We’ve determined this is not a local client, browser, or credential issue.


What changed

Microsoft has transitioned Outlook Tasks into Microsoft To Do, alongside:

*	The rollout of New Outlook
*	Updated identity and passkey-based authentication
*	Backend workload changes for Exchange mailboxes

Following this transition, Tasks / To Do are no longer available for this mailbox, indicating the Tasks workload may not be enabled at the Exchange backend after the upgrade.


Observed behavior

*	Tasks do not appear in Outlook (classic or new)
*	No Tasks options in Outlook Advanced settings
*	Microsoft To Do cannot bind to the mailbox
*	Repeated sign-in loops when accessing Tasks
*	Issue persists across browsers, devices, and Outlook versions

Installing Windows 11 Outlook does not resolve the issue, as it depends on the same Exchange configuration.


Requested action

Please verify and re-enable the Microsoft To Do / Tasks workload for the mailbox:


steve@christysigns.com

Once enabled, Tasks should immediately:

*	Appear in Outlook
*	Sync with Microsoft To Do
*	Stop authentication loops


Thank you,

 

Steve Skye

subject: Living Waters Church – Chino Valley Sign Permit Update (Electrical Permit Requirement) (01/06/25)
body:
Hi Rocky,



Quick follow-up on the Living Waters Church sign permit in Chino Valley with an important clarification from the Town (see below).


After speaking directly with Heather Narvesen, Senior Permit Technician, she confirmed:



*	The sign permit remains under review and otherwise appears ready to move forward.
*	The Town is waiting on an electrical permit for power to the sign base before they can proceed toward issuance.
*	Chino Valley requires the electrical permit to be submitted by a contractor licensed for electrical work.
*	Christy Signs is licensed as a sign contractor (C-38 classification) and is not eligible to submit the electrical permit for this scope.


Once the electrical permit is submitted by a properly licensed electrical contractor, the Town indicated the sign permit review can continue without additional major issues.


I’ve attached the current permit status report for reference. Let me know if able to be of any additional assistance.

subject: Back Nine (27544) – City of Scottsdale Corrections Issued + MSP Attached
body:
Hi Sarah,



We received the City of Scottsdale’s notification that Back Nine (Plan Check 8852-25) has completed Review Cycle 1 and is now in CORRECTIONS status. I’ve attached the correction sheets along with the Master Signage Package referenced in the City’s notes. Below is a concise breakdown of what must be addressed before the next submittal:

 

1️⃣ Provide landlord / property-management approval letter
The application is flagged as administratively incomplete because ownership approval is not yet on file. A signed approval must accompany the corrected package.

2️⃣ Update artwork and elevations per MSP standards
Key alignment items called out by the reviewer include:

*         Letter height limits — Must comply with the MSP dimensional maximums; current submittal exceeds the allowable size (see MSP pg. 2).

*         Tenant elevation formatting — Required elevation format and façade call-outs must follow MSP exhibit style (MSP pg. 12–13).

*         Hanging sign installation details — Installation height above grade and bracket mounting detail must be shown (correction sheet pg. 3).

*         Window graphic requirements
• Provide area calculations (total square footage)
• Confirm percentage of transparency / open-view requirement
• Identify material type and method of application (film vs. lettering)

3️⃣ Corrected set + checklist required for upload
Once the above items are corrected, the full package needs to be reassembled with:

*         Updated plan set

*         Landlord approval letter

*         Completed City resubmittal checklist

*         Any supplemental specifications referenced (materials, illumination specs, etc.)


I’ll prepare the actual portal resubmittal once the corrected plan set and landlord approval are in hand.


Let me know if you’d like a quick call to review the corrections together before the revisions begin.


Thanks,

subject: Notice: Copier Scan-to-Email Outage (SMTP Configuration Required)
body:
Hi Team,



I wanted to make everyone aware of a current issue with the copy machine’s scan-to-email function.



After speaking with Document Solutions of the Valley, it was confirmed that the copier’s SMTP settings are no longer valid. Previously, scanned emails were routed through an SMTP service provided by Document Solutions, but that service has expired, which is why scans are no longer reaching our email accounts.



To resolve this, the copier must be updated to use Christy Signs’ SMTP credentials. Our IT service will need to provide the correct SMTP settings for our domain before this can be completed. Once those settings are available, Document Solutions of the Valley can apply them if management chooses to proceed that way.


What to know for now

*	The copier can still scan, but scan-to-email is not functional.
*	Resolution depends on IT providing SMTP details.
*	This notice is for awareness and coordination only; it is not yet scheduled.


In the meantime, please use alternate methods to share scanned documents as needed.


Thank you, and we’ll share updates once IT guidance is available.


Best regards,

subject: Wendler Parcels — Building-Mounted EMC Question (Code Citations) (12/22/25)
body:
Hi Rocky,



We revisited this question using the Tempe Zoning & Development Code to make sure the distinction is clear now that the sign is being proposed on the building. Even if the sign is building-mounted, an electronic message center (EMC) that is visible from the freeway is not permitted by right under the current GID zoning for the Wendler parcels.  The restriction is based on sign technology and freeway orientation, not whether the sign is freestanding or attached to the building:



*	Tempe ZDC §4-902(B)(4)–(5) prohibits signs with flashing, intermittent, animated, or changeable copy, except where specifically authorized elsewhere in Chapter 9. An EMC qualifies as changeable copy and is therefore not allowed by default.
*	Tempe ZDC §4-903 (Sign Type E – Freeway-Oriented Signs) requires that any signage intended to communicate to freeway traffic be approved through a Development Agreement authorized by City Council. This section governs freeway-facing signage regardless of mounting method.
*	While wall signs are generally allowed in the GID district under §4-904, that section addresses placement and area only and does not override the electronic/changeable copy restrictions in §4-902 or the freeway-sign provisions in §4-903.
*	The larger digital and freeway monument signs along the I-10 corridor were approved decades ago under specific Development Plans and are treated as legal nonconforming signs per §4-902(E). Those approvals do not apply to the Wendler parcels.


In short:

*	Static wall signs (including internally illuminated letters) are allowed by right.
*	Electronic message centers, even when mounted on the building and visible from the freeway, would require a Development Agreement and City Council approval.


If helpful, we can add this code-based clarification directly into the Sign Ordinance Report, so it’s documented clearly for the record.


Best regards,



Steve Skye

Fax: 602-271-0433

subject: RE: Updated Sign Artwork – Prestige Home Studio (12/08/25)
body:
Hi Nassim,



Thank you for reviewing the revised artwork (see attached) and for the continued dialogue on this.


I want to clarify why the updated proposal comes in higher than expected, even with illumination removed. In this case, the primary cost driver is the total number of individual letters, not 
the logo itself. The logo has already been simplified as much as possible and is not contributing meaningfully to the increase.


With this layout, the fabrication scope requires a larger quantity of reverse channel letters, each of which must be individually fabricated, finished, mounted, and installed. That labor and material requirement remains substantial whether the letters are illuminated or non-illuminated. As a result, removing illumination reduces cost only marginally compared to the overall fabrication effort.


For clarity, pricing for this layout is as follows:

*	$11,511.62 – Fabricate and install illuminated reverse channel letter display
*	$10,268.84 – Fabricate and install non-illuminated reverse channel letter display
*	Permit fees – billed at cost
*	Staff time – $450.00


The attached artwork reflects this revised configuration and letter count.


If reducing overall cost is the priority, the most effective path would be reducing the total number of letters (for example, consolidating wording or adjusting layout), rather than focusing solely on illumination. I’m happy to explore alternate layouts with you to see if we can better align with your budget while still meeting your visual goals.


Please let me know how you’d like to proceed.


Best regards,

 

Steve Skye

Cc: Rocky Marsh <rocky@christysigns.com>
Subject: Re: [EXTERNAL] U-Haul Sahuarita - Comprehensive Sign Plan (12/08/25)

 

Steve,

 

I have provided information on the Comprehensive Sign Plan below. Please fill out the attached application as well. Planning and Zoning Commission meetings are the first Monday's of the month so February 2nd would be your goal.

In order to make that meeting we would need to have the advertisement to the newspaper approximately 3 weeks before the meeting date. Your application with all required materials needs to be submitted really by the end of this month so we can review it. If it is not in by then you are looking at the March meeting date.

 

We do not have a separate form for the Comprehensive Sign Plan. The sign code does specifically state what is required in your application, which is listed below.

 

2. Required Elements. The comprehensive sign plan shall provide the following information:

a. A design theme with illustrative examples of each sign type.

b. The location, size, height, construction materials, color, type of illumination, and orientation of all existing and proposed signs.

c. Maximum numbers of tenant panels per sign face.

d. For all freestanding signs, setbacks from right-of-way and property lines.

e. For all attached signs, clearance below and context of placement on facades.

f. Total proposed sign area per frontage, per sign type, and overall for the project.

g. Maximum allowed sign area per frontage, per sign type, and overall for the project, and explanations of how the maximums were calculated.

h. If the applicant proposes a deviation from the standards set forth in this chapter, the following additional information shall be provided:

(1) A detailed explanation of the deviations being proposed.

(2) A written justification for the deviations.

 

The code also explains what needs to be met in order to get the extra 20 percent.

 

With planning and zoning commission approval at a public hearing noticed per STC 18.91.060 <https://www.codepublishing.com/AZ/Sahuarita/#!/Sahuarita18/Sahuarita1891.html#18.91.060> (A), a comprehensive sign plan may allow signage in which the total sign area budget for each sign type and height of freestanding signs exceeds the maximum otherwise allowed by five percent for each criterion met, up to a maximum of 20 percent. In no event may the comprehensive sign plan propose signage of a type that is otherwise prohibited by this chapter, and in no event may the height, number, or size of freeway-style signs exceed the maximum otherwise allowed. Increases in sign area budgets for a sign type or freestanding sign height shall be based on the following criteria:

a. An additional five percent for use of one or a combination of the following options in all illuminated signage:

(1) Halo illumination, prohibiting the use of white or off-white/ivory light sources; or

(2) Prohibition of the use of predominantly white or off-white/ivory internally illuminated lettering, logos or trademarks.

b. An additional five percent when each sign is related to all other signs maintained on the site by the incorporation of similar or identical elements, such as materials, sign copy, letter styles, color, illumination, method of attachment, and overall presentation.

c. An additional five percent for the use of native or natural, or native- or natural-look, sign construction materials or colors that are reflective of the surrounding desert and mountain environment, the purpose of which is improved and innovative sign design and an improved image of the use or development; a minimum of 75 percent of the sign structure shall be constructed of such native or natural, or native- or natural-look, materials.

d. An additional five percent for a sign plan that relates in form, proportion, scale, color, materials, surface treatment, overall sign size, and the size and style of the lettering to the function and architectural character of the building or premises on which they will be displayed, and which provides for signs that are placed in a logical location in relation to the overall composition of the building’s facade and do not cover any key architectural features or details of the facade.

 

Additional information can be found in the Town code using the following link:

 

https://www.codepublishing.com/AZ/Sahuarita/#!/Sahuarita18/Sahuarita1879.html#18.79

Jim,

Here are the NEC notes for the freestanding electric sign at Stotz Equipment that you can drop into the project file / sheet notes.

600.4 Listing

All electric signs must be listed and labeled (typically UL 48).

600.5 Branch Circuit Requirements

A. Dedicated Circuit

*         Signs must be supplied by a dedicated branch circuit.

*         Minimum rating: 20 amps.

*         No other loads allowed on this circuit.

B. Disconnecting Means (600.6 & 600.7)
Every sign must include:

*         Disconnect switch within sight of the sign or inside the sign structure.

*         Must disconnect all ungrounded conductors.

*         Must be lockable in the open position.

600.8 Grounding & Bonding

*         The sign structure must be bonded to the equipment grounding conductor.

*         All metal parts of the freestanding sign must be bonded.

600.9 Ballasts, Transformers, and Power Supplies

If present (LED drivers, neon transformers, etc.):

*         Must be listed, accessible, and installed per manufacturer requirements.

*         Must be enclosed and protected from moisture & physical damage.

Subject: G2502-017 28085 AZ 188
Importance: High

 

Please open and read all attachments included. These attachments are your approved plans and all other required documents to go with these plans. 

All building plans attached need to be printed in color on 18”x24” minimum to 24”x36” maximum.  All calculations can be printed on 8 ½” x 11” paper, if applicable .   Deck and Solar plans will need to be on at least 11” x 17”, if applicable .  The approved site plan will need to be attached to the plans and be the 1st page of the plans. Your site plan can be printed out on 11 x 17 size paper. The approved submittal can be on 8 ½ x 11 size paper.

The stamped approved set, plans, engineering calculation, truss calculations, floor joist calculations need to be on site for every inspection. 

The Blue Cards attached must be printed in color; pg. 1,  the checklist needs to be stapled to your approved plans for the inspectors. The smaller blue card must be placed at your driveway (in a Ziplock bag or some kind of protection) for your community to know you are permitted to construct on your property. (we print them in our office on card stock paper so they last longer in the field, you may not have that option so periodically you may want to make copies of this list that the inspectors sign off on from the field, so they do not get torn and worn)

Every time you pass an inspection you will receive 180 more days on your permit. 

When we final your project we toss your plans after 180 days. So please keep a copy for your records. 

Contact the office for every inspection on your checklist above named blue cards. 

Thank you!

Subject: RE: Sign Permit Application Inquiry - LPSG 251389 (Jas Diesel) (11/20/25)

 

Hello,

the only thing the previous approval can provide is the solace that this new submittal will eventually get approved if all corrections are met.

 

Proposed sign A falls in a public utility easement. To keep sign in proposed location, please provide sign off from every utility company operating in this easement. This will also require the owner to move and reinstall this sign at their expense should any work need to be performed in this area.

 

*	You’ll need to complete a blue stake survey and contact every utility company operating in this easement for sign off to allow this ground sign here.

subject: Sign Permit Application Inquiry - LPSG 251389 (Jas Diesel) (11/20/25)
body:
Hi Jacob,



Thank you for the correction notice and the detailed review.


We want to note that the proposed ground sign was approved under a previously submitted application. Although the permit expired and we understand the need to resubmit, several of the current corrections appear to conflict with what was approved in the earlier review cycle.  For clarity, here are the items we are seeking guidance on:




________________________________

• Easement Requirement

*         The correction states: “Proposed sign A falls in a public utility easement…”

*         This issue was addressed during the original submittal, but we are unsure what documentation is now required to show proof of compliance.

*         Could you clarify what the city needs to satisfy this requirement?

________________________________

• Sign Height

*         The earlier approval included a 20' sign height.

*         The current correction states: “Please lower overall sign height to 16 feet.”

*         We are unsure how the 20' height was approved previously but is now being treated as non-compliant.

*         Could we review this to confirm whether a correction is required or whether this may be an oversight?

________________________________


Before revising or redesigning anything, we would appreciate a brief review to confirm the correct path forward and ensure full compliance.


Please let me know a convenient time to discuss, or feel free to provide clarification via email.


Thank you,

 

Steve Skye

Sent: Wednesday, November 19, 2025 3:49 PM
To: Steve Skye <steve@christysigns.com>
Subject: LPSG 251389 corr1

 

*CORRECTIONS*

Proposed sign A falls in a public utility easement. To keep sign in proposed location, please provide sign off from every utility company operating in this easement. This will also require the owner to move and reinstall this sign at their expense should any work need to be performed in this area.

 

Signs should not disturb any trees approved by the site/landscape plan for this parcel. any plans to remove or disturb trees should be approved by pdd.siteplanning@phoenix.gov <mailto:pdd.siteplanning@phoenix.gov> .

 

Proposed sign A meets the requirements for a use permit due to the use of an electronic message display. Please see attached on how to apply for your use permit on ShapePhx. The fee is $1080 and requires a public hearing that may take up to 6 weeks to schedule. Existing ZA case for previous sign has expired and requires a new zoning amendment approval.

 

Proposed sign A exceeds the maximum height allowed by sign code 705 table D1, commercial land use. Please lower overall sign height to 16 feet. To keep as proposed, submit for design review. the fee is $150; the review time is 2 weeks and requires a written narrative.

Additional reason for design review – site plan requirement. All site plans created after 1992 require ground signs to submit for design review. All reasons for design review will be included in the written narrative and will only a one-time fee.

 

Please email me when you have completed your task on projectdox.

 

Thank you,

body:
Rocky,



I took another look at the revised authorization letter from Tikova. The structure is good overall, but the last sentence introduces a concern. It states that “Tikova is the manager of Guadalupe Higley, LLC and has authority to complete the CSP on behalf of the new owners.”


Since Guadalupe Higley, LLC is no longer the property owner, this wording could create an issue with the Town of Gilbert. The authorization should clearly indicate that Tikova is granting permission for Christy Signs to act on behalf of the current ownership.


Here’s a corrected version of that paragraph that would align with the County’s ownership records and meet the Town’s requirements:



Tikova, LLC, acting with the authorization of the current property owners — Stinson Family No. 1 L.P. (Parcel 304-15-027C, 3225 E Guadalupe Rd) and FE Gilbert LLC (Parcel 304-15-027D, 759 N Higley Rd) — hereby authorizes Christy Signs to prepare, process, and submit the Comprehensive Sign Plan (CSP) with the Town of Gilbert on behalf of the ownership of record.


Once updated with this language, the letter should be fully acceptable for submittal.


Thanks,

 

Steve Skye

subject: Sign Permit Application Report - Higley & Guadalupe Comprehensive Sign Plan (CSP) (11/07/25)
body:
Hi Rocky,



I wanted to provide an update on the Higley & Guadalupe Comprehensive Sign Plan (CSP) submitted to the Town of Gilbert under Plan Number PDR-2025-00158.


All required materials have been uploaded, and the application is officially in “Submitted” status as of November 5, 2025. The Town’s portal currently shows the project as 17% complete, pending assignment to a planner for initial review.


Per the Town of Gilbert Design Review – Comprehensive Sign Program Administrative Process Guide (see attached), the next steps in the process include:

*	Administrative Completeness Review: Staff will first confirm that all submittal materials meet checklist requirements (property owner authorization, project narrative, site and sign plans, materials board, etc.).
*	First Review Cycle: Once deemed complete, the plan moves into technical review. Staff may return the submittal for revisions if any corrections are needed.
*	Administrative Approval: Most CSPs are approved at staff level. However, the Planning Manager may refer the case to the Design Review Board if any elements warrant additional consideration
*	Inactive Case Closure: If no response is provided within 180 days after Town comments, the case automatically closes.


Given the Town’s current review timelines, we can expect initial staff feedback within approximately 3–4 weeks. I’ll continue to monitor the record and provide updates as the review advances.


Best regards,

 

Steve Skye

Subject: Signage Limitations for Wendler Parcels – City of Tempe (GID Zoning) 

 

Hi Rocky,

I wanted to update you on the signage restrictions for the Wendler parcels (4415 & 4625 S Wendler Dr, Tempe), based on our review of the City of Tempe Zoning and Development Code and confirmation from Mike Scarpitta of the Tempe Sign Department.


Both parcels are zoned GID (General Industrial District) and are not part of any PAD or Development Plan. As such, they are limited to standard monument-style freestanding signs under Tempe ZDC §§ 4-901–4-904.

Here are the key points:

*	Maximum sign height: 8 ft
*	Maximum sign area: 24 sq ft per face
*	Type: Monument or architectural base design (masonry/stucco finish to match building)
*	Freeway/high-profile signs: Only permitted through a recorded Development Plan or PAD overlay—these Wendler parcels do not qualify under current zoning.
*	Address numerals: Minimum 6″ high required on the base.


Mike confirmed that the larger “freeway monument” signs along the I-10 corridor were approved decades ago as part of their original Development Plans and are effectively grandfathered. 

The Wendler properties were not included in those agreements, so the City will enforce the 8' / 24 sq ft limitation.


Attached is the full Sign Ordinance Report – Tempe Wendler Parcels (GID) summarizing these findings, citations, and code references for our records.


Best regards,

Hi Sarah,

Thanks again for marking up the brand book—that’s exactly what we needed to keep things moving. I’ve attached a one-page Information Sheet on NEC 600 for reference, which summarizes the code requirements inspectors are looking for.  To clarify your two questions:

3. Dedicated 20A Branch Circuit
You’re right—the electrician ultimately provides and labels the circuit. But under NEC 600.5(A), every sign must be supplied by a dedicated 20A branch circuit

Inspectors want to see this noted on the plans, so it doesn’t get overlooked in the field, even if it isn’t a fabrication detail.


4. Grounding/Bonding
This is about ensuring all metal parts of the sign and raceways are tied together and properly grounded. NEC 600.7 requires metallic sign enclosures and equipment to be bonded to ground.  In practice, this means including a note that a grounding conductor and bonding jumpers will be installed so the sign is safe under fault conditions.


So, while these items are implemented by the electrician, the city expects them to be called out on the drawings for code compliance.


Please see the attached information sheet for a clear summary of the requirements.

subject: Power Requirements and Electrical Coordination – Freestanding Sign (10/23/25)
body:
Hi Aaron,



I’m glad to hear the artwork and proposed design meet your expectations.


For the new freestanding sign, a dedicated 120V / 20-amp circuit will be required at the base of the sign. This circuit will supply power for the internal LED illumination and must comply with the National Electrical Code (NEC) Article 600 (Electric Signs and Outline Lighting).

Key provisions include:

*	NEC 600.5(A) – Each sign must be supplied by its own branch circuit.
*	NEC 600.6(A)(1) – A disconnecting means must be installed within sight of the sign.
*	NEC 600.7(A) – Proper grounding and bonding are required for all metallic parts.


Our installation will include a junction box and weather-rated disconnect switch mounted at the base of the sign.

We recommend having your electrician provide:

*	A dedicated 20A circuit from the building’s main panel to the sign base.
*	A time clock or photo control near the breaker panel where the power run originates — this allows automatic on/off control for the sign lighting.


Once the circuit is in place, our team will make the final internal connections during installation and test all components.


Please let me know if you’d like us to coordinate directly with your electrician or provide a connection diagram for reference.


Warm regards,

 

Steve Skye

subject: FWD: Correction Notice – Drive-Thru Sign Height & Spacing (Scooter’s #2597) (10/21/25)

Hi Pedro,



Forwarding the latest correction notice from the City of Phoenix below. As noted by the reviewer (Anthony Daviss), the drive-thru signs must be included in the application and are limited to a maximum height of 3 feet unless compliant with Table D1 of the Phoenix Sign Ordinance (attached).


Per Table D1, any drive-thru sign exceeding 3 feet in height must maintain a minimum spacing of 100 feet from other ground signs.

Hi Pedro,



Looping you in with the latest status and the thread attached.



Where things stand

*         Status: “Applicant Resubmit” (awaiting City confirmation on our last submittal).

*         What we submitted: Updated freestanding sign construction documents showing the setback measured from the curb/driveway, per the field inspector’s 9/11/25 note. These were uploaded to ProjectDox on 09/12/25.

*         Why the confusion: It appears there was a misfire on the City’s end — they may not have realized that our resubmittal already included the requested driveway setback measurement. We’ve clarified this in our recent follow-up.


Current action
Anthony Daviss, the City of Phoenix Sign Inspector, is reviewing the freestanding sign package (with the curb-based measurements) to verify that it aligns with their request.


What’s next

*         Awaiting Mr. Daviss’ review and confirmation that the ground sign documentation is complete.

*         The wall sign has pre-approval and we’re waiting for formal approval from the City.


I’ll update you as soon as we receive acknowledgment or if any additional information is requested.

subject: Super 8 Motel – LED Retrofit & Photocell Replacement (WO #27425)
body:
Hi Hitesh,



Thank you for the order to retrofit your existing fluorescent sign to LED. As discussed, we’ll also replace the failed photocells as part of the scope, so the sign operates reliably at dusk/dawn.  To finalize everything, please:



1.	Endorse the agreement (attached estimate – WO #27425). 
2.	Complete the Credit Card Authorization Form and return it with the last four digits and billing zip so we can process the deposit. 
3.	You’ll also find the deposit invoice attached for your records. 


Once we receive the signed estimate and payment authorization, we’ll confirm scheduling and lead time.


Warm regards,

body:
Hi Tony and Marc,



Thank you both for clarifying — it’s much appreciated.


Attached is our updated file for the ground sign, which includes the revised setback measurement from the driveway rather than the property line, per the field inspector’s notes dated 9/11/25. This revision was uploaded to ProjectDox on 09/12/25, as shown in the attached screenshot. The site map is located on page 2 of the construction documents for reference.


To our understanding, all required documentation for the freestanding sign have been submitted. If there’s a contact within the sign review division who could provide a brief status update or explain typical timelines, I’d deeply appreciate it.

Hi Steve,



I spoke with Kimberly Pippin at the Town of Queen Creek this morning (480-358-3003) regarding the awnings. She confirmed that awnings fall under the building permit category, not sign permits, and therefore would require a general contractor’s license.


Since our ROC # 071084 classification does not cover building permits, we would not be able to apply for the awning portion directly.


We will proceed with the flagpole permit (B25-2353), which remains active under the sign permit scope, but the awnings will need to be handled under the building permit process—either by the GC or another licensed contractor qualified for that scope.

Main thing right now really is to just get signage up on our buildings. Our building is up and bare, and we are opening soon. We can wait for the monument sign if that is the harder thing to run through the process. '

Subject: Re: Hi Anthony! Checking in, and introducing myself. LPSG 251110

 

Hi Tony and Steve, 

 

Good morning! TGIM!

 

Really appreciate all the quick replies.

 

I am still unclear. It appears its same response that triggered my original inquiry. All I know is that the project is 'in review'. This is what Steve had let me know and he shared that he had no additional info. So, I was reaching out to get more context. I don't have any color or detail, timeline or idea of process. Kind of feels like a black hole, so just seeking to understand. That was my purpose for reaching out. Anthony: is there someone on your team that could help me walk me through where we are at and what to expect next beyond that we are just 'in review' until we are not' which is what I feel is all I have. It's sad seeing our building up with no signage.

 

And again, I completely understand that review times can vary and that your team is surely managing a large volume of projects. However, at this point, we’re struggling to get clarity on the status, next steps, and expected timing.

Our signage partner and our team have both been checking the system, but the only update available continues to show “in review.” We’d be grateful for any additional context or insight you could provide—such as where the project currently stands in the process, whether any feedback or revisions are pending, and what typical turnaround times are at this stage.

My goal isn’t simply to push for speed (although we are eager for signs, at minimum for the bare building) but to better understand the process and expectations so that we can plan future projects more effectively. We want to ensure we’re doing our part to avoid similar bottlenecks and that future openings don’t occur with finished buildings sitting without signage for weeks.

If there’s a contact within the sign review division who could provide a brief status update or explain typical timelines, I’d deeply appreciate it.

Thank you for the important work your team does in keeping the City of Phoenix running smoothly. I know how many requests come through your office, and I’m grateful for your time and any guidance you can offer.

Kind regards,

Alex

subject: RE: Update -  Scooters #2597 - Phoenix, AZ
body:
Hi Alex and Pedro,



At this time, we’ve still received no response or update from the City of Phoenix regarding the Scooters #2597 sign permit.


The only other contact available beyond the assigned inspector (Anthony “Tony” Daviss) is the Sign Services Department directly at (602) 495-0301 or pdd.signservices@phoenix.gov. 
However, in my experience, they primarily accept voicemails and rarely provide direct updates by phone, so I’m not confident that would yield any quicker results (I checked this morning).


We’ll continue to monitor for any movement and follow up as needed. I’ll notify you immediately once we receive confirmation from the city.


Best regards,

 

Steve Skye

Fax: 602-271-0433

Subject: Update - Scooters #2597 - Phoenix, AZ

 

Hi Steve,

 

                I know we have spoke every few days about checking in and last we spoke we are still in review on the portal.   Can you be sure to include all on email with any updates and see what our status is today.

 

If you have any other contacts with city other than Anthony Davis please share.

 



	
Anthony “Tony” Daviss

Sign Inspector, Planning and Development Department Signs

Office: 602-534-3481

E-mail: anthony.daviss@phoenix.gov <mailto:anthony.daviss@phoenix.gov> 

​​Signs​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​ | City of Phoenix <https://www.phoenix.gov/administration/departments/pdd/commercial-multifamily-building/commercial-plan-reviews-permits/signs.html> 

Chapter 7 Development Standards of General Applicability | Phoenix Zoning Ordinance <https://phoenix.municipal.codes/ZO/705> 

 

 

Hi Alex,

 

                We are for sure keeping you on all emails as you can see below.  

 

Again, per local sign co. who has past experiences on permits - Phoenix operates very differently. Their review staff is not receptive to phone calls or direct inquiries—voicemails and emails often go unanswered—and, candidly, pressing too hard can make the process more difficult.

 

Having said that.  Did you make any phone calls to anyone on your side yet, local rep. or city mayor office, etc.?

 

Best,

 

Pedro Vargas

Account Executive

 <http://www.omahaneon.com/> 

1120 N. 18th St.

Omaha, NE 68102

Office 402-341-6077 Ext. 2207

 

 

Good morning, Alex,

 

I completely understand your concern. In most jurisdictions I would be making those calls and pushing for updates, but unfortunately Phoenix operates very differently. Their review staff is not receptive to phone calls or direct inquiries—voicemails and emails often go unanswered—and, candidly, pressing too hard can make the process more difficult.

 

It’s frustrating, but from experience I’ve found that the best path with Phoenix is to let their process run its course. All required documents have been submitted, and the application is in their system—it’s just a matter of when it comes up in their queue.

 

I’ll continue checking the portal daily and will notify you immediately when there’s movement. I share your urgency and will do everything possible to keep this on track, but I want to avoid doing anything that could risk slowing down the review further.

 

Best regards,

subject: Dunkin sign questions | Project 62167
body:
Hi Adam,

Thank you for sending the revised drawings and update. We’ve completed our internal review of the latest Dunkin’ Avondale sign package, and our Electrical & Sign Code Compliance Report is attached for your reference.  Overall, the submittal aligns with Avondale’s C-3/PAD sign standards and meets the applicable NEC and UL requirements for illuminated signage. The proposed wall sign dimensions and placements are within the allowable area and consistent with prior approvals.  However, as noted in our report:

*	The disconnect switch locations and bonding/grounding notes required by NEC 600.6(A)(1) and 600.7(A) are not currently shown on the electrical drawings. These need to be added before the next permit resubmittal.
*	All metallic sign housings, raceways, and conduits must be bonded to the equipment grounding conductor, and each illuminated sign must include a lockable disconnect switch within sight of the unit.
*	Once these items are incorporated, the package will be fully compliant and ready for city review.


Regarding the clearance bar, our understanding is that Avondale’s code restricts freestanding drive-thru accessories with moving or swing elements, which is why the clearance bar was previously disallowed. We defer to Cole for final confirmation, but a static, non-lettered clearance device may be acceptable under current code if treated as a protective structure rather than a sign.


Please see the attached Dunkin’ Avondale Electrical & Sign Code Compliance Report (PDF) for our detailed findings.


Best regards,

 

Steve Skye

Hi Rebekah,



Thank you for confirming — that helps clarify the functionality side. From what you’ve described, it sounds like Cirrus units can technically operate at either Level 3 or Level 4, depending on how the display content is managed rather than any hardware limitation.


For our permitting purposes, I’ll be explaining to the customer that Level 3 is limited to static and transitional content only — meaning no moving animation or full-motion video — while Level 4 introduces dynamic video and animation elements that typically require special use or conditional approval under Maricopa County’s electronic sign code.


I’ll handle the code interpretation and customer guidance from here, but your confirmation on how the Cirrus software treats transitions versus animation was exactly what I needed.


Appreciate your help,

subject: Southwest Industrial Rigging – Pole Sign Compliance (IND-2, Maricopa County) (10/07/25)
body:
Hi Aaron,



Thanks for sending the concept package. I reviewed your proposed pole sign against Maricopa County (Unincorporated) IND-2 standards for 4705 S 35th Ave (APN 105-68-002U). Here’s the summary.


Site & Zoning

*         Jurisdiction/Zoning: Unincorporated Maricopa County, IND-2 (Light Industrial) — signage is regulated by the County Zoning Ordinance (not City of Phoenix). 


County Allowances for a Freestanding (Pole) Sign – IND-2

*         Max height: 24 ft overall.

*         Max area per face: 150 sq ft (double-faced counts one face).

*         Quantity: 1 pole sign per driveway, with ≥200 ft separation on the same parcel.

*         Setbacks/Safety: Entirely on private property; outside right-of-way and sight-visibility triangles.

*         Lighting/EMD: Internal/external illumination OK; no flashing/animated/video. EMD allowed (Levels 1–3); Level 4 (full animation/video) is prohibited. 


How the Concept Compares (what you sent)

*         Configuration: Single pole sign with a main display and an EMD cabinet noted at 8' W × 4' H (≈32 sq ft) — the EMD portion is comfortably within the County’s per-face limit. We’ll confirm the total sign face area once final cabinet dimensions are locked, to ensure ≤150 sq ft per face. 

*         Height: Concept appears to target a mid-teen to sub-24' overall height; we’ll keep ≤24 ft on the final. If any segment of the installation ends up within 200 ft of a residential zone, a 12' cap applies at the boundary and then steps up 1' per 5' of additional distance (we’ll verify buffer in the staking plan). 

*         Quantity/Placement: One pole sign planned; we’ll site it outside ROW/SVT and confirm ≥200 ft spacing from any other freestanding signs on the parcel. 

*         Lighting/EMD Behavior: We’ll specify static image sequencing that complies with EMD Level 1–3 (no full-motion video), plus automatic night dimming. 


Quick Compliance Matrix

*         Zoning District: IND-2 → ✅ matches site. 

*         Height ≤ 24': To be held in stamped drawings. 

*         Area ≤ 150 sq ft/face: To be confirmed once cabinet dims are finalized (EMD = 32 sq ft ✔). 

*         One per driveway & ≥200' separation: Planned; verify during staking. 

*         Setbacks/SVT clear: Will confirm with survey base. 

*         Illumination/EMD Levels 1–3 only: Compliant by spec (no video/animation). 


Next Steps

1.    Finalize cabinet dimensions so we can certify ≤150 sq ft/face (EMD already within limits). 

2.    Stake location & survey check (ROW/SVT, driveway spacing, residential buffer). 

3.    Engineer footing & structural set for submittal.

4.    County permit package (Maricopa County P&D) with photometric/EMD dimming notes and static display policy. 


I’ve attached our Zoning Report and Sign Ordinance Report for your records; they’ll travel with the permit submittal. 


If you want, I can prepare a shop-drawing revision so everything is “permit-ready.”


Thanks,

 

Steve Skye

Hi Sarah,

Thanks again for marking up the brand book—that’s exactly what we needed to keep things moving. I’ve attached a one-page Information Sheet on NEC 600 for reference, which summarizes the code requirements inspectors are looking for.  To clarify your two questions:

3. Dedicated 20A Branch Circuit
You’re right—the electrician ultimately provides and labels the circuit. But under NEC 600.5(A), every sign must be supplied by a dedicated 20A branch circuit

Inspectors want to see this noted on the plans, so it doesn’t get overlooked in the field, even if it isn’t a fabrication detail.


4. Grounding/Bonding
This is about ensuring all metal parts of the sign and raceways are tied together and properly grounded. NEC 600.7 requires metallic sign enclosures and equipment to be bonded to ground.  In practice, this means including a note that a grounding conductor and bonding jumpers will be installed so the sign is safe under fault conditions.


So, while these items are implemented by the electrician, the city expects them to be called out on the drawings for code compliance.


Please see the attached information sheet for a clear summary of the requirements.

4. Grounding/Bonding
This is about ensuring all metal parts of the sign and raceways are tied together and properly grounded. NEC 600.7 requires metallic sign enclosures and equipment to be bonded to ground.  In practice, this means including a note that a grounding conductor and bonding jumpers will be installed so the sign is safe under fault conditions.


So, while these items are implemented by the electrician, the city expects them to be called out on the drawings for code compliance.


Please see the attached information sheet for a clear summary of the requirements.

	Hi Alex,
	
	

	I want to give you a clearer sense of what we deal with when working with the City of Phoenix. Unlike many other jurisdictions, they are very rigid in their approach and don’t engage in back-and-forth conversations about “what if” or “how soon.”  Here’s a direct example from one of their sign inspectors (Anthony “Tony” Daviss) concerning this project (see attached):
	
	

	“My apologies, I don’t do hypotheticals. Submit what you have and I will review. As long as you follow the guidelines that was sent to you then you should be fine. If you are trying to go, however so small, different then what is allowed then its not allowed. They are pretty clear on what is required for a ground sign. Basically, any ‘what if I do this’ questions are denied if it’s not what the overlay states that can be had. Simplest I can put it.”

	
	This is typical of Phoenix’s communication style. They expect complete submittals, won’t speculate, and often provide minimal feedback outside of official redlines. That’s why I’ve been cautious about “pushing” them too aggressively—it usually doesn’t speed things up and can actually make things harder.

	
	That said, we will continue logging calls and emails to keep a record of our follow-ups, even if most go unanswered. All required documents for Scooters #2597 are in their system, and at this stage, it’s simply waiting for the project to come up in their queue.

Subject: Urgent Compliance Concern – Permit Fee Payment Practices & Risk to Contracting License 

 

Dear Christy Signs Management,

I am writing to formally express my deep concern regarding a recurring and escalating issue: permits being approved by municipalities but not paid for prior to installation. This practice exposes Christy Signs to serious risk, including potential investigation fees, municipal penalties, and most critically, the loss of our contractor’s license.


Today, we received a direct warning from Fernando Lovett, a City of Phoenix Sign Inspector, regarding our work at Jason’s Deli (10217 N Metrocenter Pkwy, Permits T-157163 & T-157164). In his words, this was “the last time” he will refrain from issuing an investigation fee. His email (see attached) made it clear that if this happens again, there will be financial penalties and the possibility of more severe actions by the City.


This is not an isolated incident.

Over the past several months, I have sent continuous updates by email documenting permit statuses, including explicit notes regarding fees due and pending payments. Unfortunately, these updates are often unread or rarely acted upon despite their significance. This lack of timely response directly results in situations like today’s, where our crews are installing signage without properly cleared permits.


To be absolutely clear:

*	I am fulfilling my responsibility by tracking, reporting, and communicating permit status and fee requirements in a timely manner.
*	The decision not to act on this information rests outside of my role and control.
*	I must therefore formally document this concern to protect both the company and myself.


Immediate Recommendations:

1.	Establish a strict policy requiring all permit fees to be paid before scheduling any installation.
2.	Assign a single point of accountability for fee payments to prevent confusion or oversight.
3.	Implement a visible tracking system (dashboard or shared file) showing unpaid permits and deadlines so there is no ambiguity.


Without immediate action, we risk more than just investigation fees. Persistent non-payment could be interpreted by the city as willful noncompliance, which can jeopardize our contractor’s license and relationships with municipalities across the Valley.


Please treat this matter with the highest level of urgency. I suggest we meet to establish the proper corrective action.


Respectfully,

 

Steve Skye

Office: 602-242-4488

Fax: 602-271-0433

Email: steve@christysigns.com <mailto:steve@christysigns.com> 

Web: www.ChristySigns.com <http://www.christysigns.com/>

	I want to give you a clearer sense of what we deal with when working with the City of Phoenix. Unlike many other jurisdictions, they are very rigid in their approach and don’t engage in back-and-forth conversations about “what if” or “how soon.”  Here’s a direct example from one of their sign inspectors (Anthony “Tony” Daviss) concerning this project (see attached):
	
	
	

	“My apologies, I don’t do hypotheticals. Submit what you have and I will review. As long as you follow the guidelines that was sent to you then you should be fine. If you are trying to go, however so small, different then what is allowed then its not allowed. They are pretty clear on what is required for a ground sign. Basically, any ‘what if I do this’ questions are denied if it’s not what the overlay states that can be had. Simplest I can put it.”

	
	This is typical of Phoenix’s communication style. They expect complete submittals, won’t speculate, and often provide minimal feedback outside of official redlines. That’s why I’ve been cautious about “pushing” them too aggressively—it usually doesn’t speed things up and can actually make things harder.

subject: RE: Update -  Scooters #2597 - Phoenix, AZ
body:
Hi Alex,



I want to give you a clearer sense of what we deal with when working with the City of Phoenix. Unlike many other jurisdictions, they are very rigid in their approach and don’t engage in back-and-forth conversations about “what if” or “how soon.”  Here’s a direct example from one of their sign inspectors (Anthony “Tony” Daviss) concerning this project (see attached):



“My apologies, I don’t do hypotheticals. Submit what you have and I will review. As long as you follow the guidelines that was sent to you then you should be fine. If you are trying to go, however so small, different then what is allowed then its not allowed. They are pretty clear on what is required for a ground sign. Basically, any ‘what if I do this’ questions are denied if it’s not what the overlay states that can be had. Simplest I can put it.”


This is typical of Phoenix’s communication style. They expect complete submittals, won’t speculate, and often provide minimal feedback outside of official redlines. That’s why I’ve been cautious about “pushing” them too aggressively—it usually doesn’t speed things up and can actually make things harder.


That said, we will continue logging calls and emails to keep a record of our follow-ups, even if most go unanswered. All required documents for Scooters #2597 are in their system, and at this stage, it’s simply waiting for the project to come up in their queue.


I’ll keep monitoring the portal daily and will notify you and the team immediately when we see movement. I share your urgency and will continue doing everything possible to keep this moving.


Best regards,

 

Steve Skye

Fax: 602-271-0433

Alex

subject: Urgent Compliance Concern – Permit Fee Payment Practices & Risk to Contracting License
body:
Dear Christy Signs Management,



I am writing to formally express my deep concern regarding a recurring and escalating issue: permits being approved by municipalities but not paid for prior to installation. This practice exposes Christy Signs to serious risk, including potential investigation fees, municipal penalties, and most critically, the loss of our contractor’s license.


Today, we received a direct warning from Fernando Lovett, a City of Phoenix Sign Inspector, regarding our work at Jason’s Deli (10217 N Metrocenter Pkwy, Permits T-157163 & T-157164). In his words, this was “the last time” he will refrain from issuing an investigation fee. His email (see attached) made it clear that if this happens again, there will be financial penalties and the possibility of more severe actions by the City.


This is not an isolated incident.

Over the past several months, I have sent continuous updates by email documenting permit statuses, including explicit notes regarding fees due and pending payments. Unfortunately, these updates are often unread or rarely acted upon despite their significance. This lack of timely response directly results in situations like today’s, where our crews are installing signage without properly cleared permits.


To be absolutely clear:

*	I am fulfilling my responsibility by tracking, reporting, and communicating permit status and fee requirements in a timely manner.
*	The decision not to act on this information rests outside of my role and control.
*	I must therefore formally document this concern to protect both the company and myself.


Immediate Recommendations:

1.	Establish a strict policy requiring all permit fees to be paid before scheduling any installation.
2.	Assign a single point of accountability for fee payments to prevent confusion or oversight.
3.	Implement a visible tracking system (dashboard or shared file) showing unpaid permits and deadlines so there is no ambiguity.


Without immediate action, we risk more than just investigation fees. Persistent non-payment could be interpreted by the city as willful noncompliance, which can jeopardize our contractor’s license and relationships with municipalities across the Valley.


Please treat this matter with the highest level of urgency. I suggest we meet to establish the proper corrective action.


Respectfully,

 

Steve Skye

Fax: 602-271-0433

Email: steve@christysigns.com <mailto:steve@christysigns.com> 

Web: www.ChristySigns.com <http://www.christysigns.com/>

Good morning, Alex,

 

I completely understand your concern. In most jurisdictions I would be making those calls and pushing for updates, but unfortunately Phoenix operates very differently. Their review staff is not receptive to phone calls or direct inquiries—voicemails and emails often go unanswered—and, candidly, pressing too hard can make the process more difficult.

 

It’s frustrating, but from experience I’ve found that the best path with Phoenix is to let their process run its course. All required documents have been submitted, and the application is in their system—it’s just a matter of when it comes up in their queue.

 

I’ll continue checking the portal daily and will notify you immediately when there’s movement. I share your urgency and will do everything possible to keep this on track, but I want to avoid doing anything that could risk slowing down the review further.

Hi Rachael,

Happy Friday !

 

Thank you for sending over the additional drawings. I reviewed them, and I see that the flagpole location is noted on the site plan. That said, since this application is solely for the flagpole, I think it’s best if we streamline the resubmittal package, so it only includes details relevant to that scope. Anything referencing the other signs will likely distract the reviewer and could slow the process down.

 

The Town of Queen Creek specifically asked that the signage and flagpole be submitted under two separate applications (see attached emails). The flagpole review is being handled by a different department than the signs, so any crossover references to signage in the plan set may throw them off.

Hi Sarah,

Thanks again for marking up the brand book—that’s exactly what we needed to keep things moving. I’ve attached a one-page Information Sheet on NEC 600 for reference, which summarizes the code requirements inspectors are looking for.  To clarify your two questions:

3. Dedicated 20A Branch Circuit
You’re right—the electrician ultimately provides and labels the circuit. But under NEC 600.5(A), every sign must be supplied by a dedicated 20A branch circuit

Inspectors want to see this noted on the plans, so it doesn’t get overlooked in the field, even if it isn’t a fabrication detail.


4. Grounding/Bonding
This is about ensuring all metal parts of the sign and raceways are tied together and properly grounded. NEC 600.7 requires metallic sign enclosures and equipment to be bonded to ground.  In practice, this means including a note that a grounding conductor and bonding jumpers will be installed so the sign is safe under fault conditions.


So, while these items are implemented by the electrician, the city expects them to be called out on the drawings for code compliance.


Please see the attached information sheet for a clear summary of the requirements.


Best regards,

Thanks for sending over the revised artwork set. After reviewing the updates, I wanted to flag two details that might cause issues during city review:



A – Page 2 (E1):
The building dimension endpoints are partially blocked by the “Existing” callout. This could make it unclear to the planner what those markers designate. It may help to adjust the placement, so the dimensions are fully visible.

The proposed tenant panels specify black vinyl, but they don’t indicate the use of day/night perforated vinyl. If these adjustments are made, I think the submittal will be much stronger going into the next round.
